title: Furry Airline Pilots Are Just Minding Their Own Business
author: Ej Dickson
text: The greatest threat to humanity’s survival isn’t climate change, nor is it AI. It’s airline pilots who like dressing up as hot cartoon foxes.That seemed to be the takeaway from a bizarre speech made last week by Alabama Republican Tommy Tuberville on the Senate floor last week. During a lengthy anti-trans rant about “gender confusion,” Tuberville started pontificating on the furry fandom, a subculture consisting of people who enjoy drawing and dressing as anthropomorphized animals. “Many airline pilots, flight attendants, and air traffic controllers are part of the furry community,” Tuberville alleged. “Lord help us. It’s terrifying when you think about this.”Don't just keep up. Get ahead—with our biggest stories, handpicked for you each day.By signing up, you agree to our user agreement (including class action waiver and arbitration provisions), and acknowledge our privacy policy.To bolster his point, he later posted a viral audio clip of airline pilots at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport meowing and barking at each other over the radio, though there is no evidence that the pilots in question were furries; the video was possibly a reference to a joke in the 2001 movie Super Troopers. “When you walk onto a commercial flight, it’s possible that the pilot flying your plane could have a deranged fetish of dressing up like an animal,” Tuberville said. (Interest in the furry fandom is not necessarily sexual, nor do all furries dress up as animals.)Featured VideoAI Researcher Answers: Is AI’s Existential Threat Real?Tuberville’s tirade went viral, with everyone from Jimmy Kimmel to The Daily Show weighing in on the absurdity of his remarks. But there was one detail largely omitted from the coverage: on at least one point, Tuberville was (kind of) correct.“It’s definitely something we’ve talked about before, why there are so many furries in the aviation community,” says Toby, a professional flying instructor who has been running a flight school for the past eight years; he is also a prominent member of the fandom whose fursona (the fandom’s term for an animal-inspired alter ego) is a wolf.Vulan, who works as a pilot for a major American airline, agreed. (Due to the stigma associated with the community, all of the furries I spoke with requested they be referred to by their fursonas rather than their real names.) Vulan, who uses they/them pronouns and whose fursona is of a fox, runs a group chat for furries in aviation—one of nearly a dozen that they know of. “It’s kind of a big deal in the furry fandom because it’s such an odd, out-of-left-field thing,” they say of the overrepresentation of furries within the air travel industry.Given its taboo nature, as well as the general dearth of data surrounding the fandom, there aren’t really many reliable numbers regarding furry employment. But the aviation industry does appear to be fairly strongly represented within the fandom. Toby hosts aviation panels at furry conventions, and he says that they are among the most popular events, with recent ones attracting upwards of 400 attendees. All fursonas, he says, are represented, though airline pilots “do tend to favor birds.”Most PopularPoliticsThe White House Is Starting to Panic Over the MidtermsBy Hugo LowellGearAmazon’s New Kindle Lineup Is Lighter, Thinner, and More MetalBy Julian ChokkattuGearCasio’s Crystal G-Shock Is the Most Expensive Ever MadeBy Jeremy WhiteGearBose Brought Back Wired Headphones, and Teens Are to ThankBy Harry RabinowitzOne furry who worked for four years at an airport kiosk says he knew of a number of other furry employees during his time there, including a baggage handler who had a tattoo of his fursona. “Some people are more vocal about it than others, but in my experience most don't talk about it,” he told me.Vulan says that at their airline alone, they know of “at least 40” other self-identified furries, from pilots to baggage handlers to air traffic controllers. It’s not, however, something they discuss openly in the workplace. “I don’t feel the need to be represented at work, and I don’t know anyone who feels that way,” they say. “I think everybody understands this is something we enjoy at home, and we're not asking to bring it into work, just like we're not asking anybody else to bring their home life into work if they don't want to.”Still, the question remains: Why does there appear to be so much crossover between the furry community and those who work in the friendly skies? Generally speaking, there is an “overlap between furries and transit nerds,” says Patch O’Furr, the editor-in-chief of the furry fandom publication Dogpatch Press. “It's a meta fandom full of roleplay so imaginative that it goes beyond species, so you get lots of people with intense special interests.”Some furries I spoke to cited the popularity of famous anthropomorphic pilots, such as the titular character—a half-man half-pig—in the 1992 Miyazaki film Porco Rosso (Italian for red pig), or the bear Baloo from the 1990s Disney cartoon TaleSpin, as having sparked a childhood interest in aviation. Others pointed to the preponderance of neurodivergent furries within the fandom, many of whom may consider aviation among their specific obsessions—though it’s worth noting the medical requirements for becoming an FAA-licensed pilot are extremely stringent, and neurodevelopmental disorder diagnoses like autism or ADHD can present barriers.Most PopularPoliticsThe White House Is Starting to Panic Over the MidtermsBy Hugo LowellGearAmazon’s New Kindle Lineup Is Lighter, Thinner, and More MetalBy Julian ChokkattuGearCasio’s Crystal G-Shock Is the Most Expensive Ever MadeBy Jeremy WhiteGearBose Brought Back Wired Headphones, and Teens Are to ThankBy Harry RabinowitzThe correlation between furries and the aviation industry may also partially stem from the fact that both involve heavy travel—many furries spend months ping-ponging across the country, going from con to con—and an intense level of interest. “For most of us in aviation, it’s not just a job, it’s a passion,” says Toby. “It’s not as plug-and-play as many other kinds of jobs, it’s a way of life. And I think the kind of mind that is attracted to aviation is the same kind of person that would be attracted to the furry fandom.”The often misunderstood furry fandom has been subject to a slew of attacks from the right over the past few years, mostly as a proxy to culture wars about LGBTQ people. In 2024, right-wing commentator Megyn Kelly amplified a false rumor that furry students at a Utah middle school were engaging in animalistic behavior like biting and scratching; viral footage of a protest linked to the issue led to the school getting bomb threats. And in 2022, a GOP lawmaker had to publicly apologize after promoting a debunked conspiracy theory that public schools were putting litter boxes in classrooms to cater to students who had started self-identifying as furries.With his unhinged ravings about “gender confusion”-afflicted furry pilots terrorizing the airwaves with perverse meowing, Tuberville, who did not immediately respond to a request for comment, appears to have been attempting to resurrect this type of moral panic—perhaps not coincidentally, just in time for the midterm elections. But the general public, which largely reacted to his comments with ridicule, doesn’t seem to be buying it. Nor, for that matter, are the furry pilots themselves, who shared Tuberville’s rant within their group texts with eye roll emojis.“We’re furries at home, and we’re airline pilots at work, and these are two separate things,” says Vulan. “I would never ask somebody to dig up their personal life at work, and I don’t think anybody wants us to do that, either.” Plus, they note, it would be impossible for them to wear their fur suit in the cockpit: “mine has terrible vision.”
